declarations.documentation:
Get a usable Google access token — the capability the tools require (`with … credential`), served by
`provider`. Each ask resolves the provider's named credential through the runtime (`oauth.token`), which
owns the stored token and its refresh; the result is a `string of private` and flows only toward the
`Bearer` header. A credential that needs a human never throws — the ask parks the run on a
`prelude.oauth.authorize` escalation and resumes once the browser flow completes — while a transient
resolution failure throws `oauth.server_error` at the provider.
declarations.name: credential
declarations.signature: request credential() -> string of private

declarations.checkedType: agent(continuation: agent(value: null) -> T0 with credential | E1, source: env | oauth) -> T0 with throw[missing_secret | server_error] | E1 | io
declarations.documentation:
Provide the Google credential for the extent of the continuation, from @source@:
`use gmail.provider(source = credentials.oauth(name = "google"))` — the same stored Google credential
`google_calendar` uses, given a Gmail scope. Resolution happens on every `credential` ask, so this
provider holds no secret and keeps no state.
declarations.name: provider
declarations.signature: agent provider[R, effect E](source: credentials.source, continuation: agent(value: null) -> R with {...E, credential}) -> R with E | io | prelude.throw[env.missing_secret | oauth.server_error]

declarations.checkedType: agent(body: unknown, context: string, method: string, url: string) -> unknown with credential | throw[api_error | auth_error | fetch_error | parse_error] | io
declarations.documentation:
Issue an authenticated Gmail API call — @method@ to @url@ with @body@ (a value tree, or `null` for a
call carrying no document) — and return the reply parsed as JSON, or `null` for an empty one. Every
endpoint in this package goes through here: `google_common.call` with this package's `credential` ask
added. A non-2xx becomes `http.api_failure` (401/403 → `http.auth_error`, else `http.api_error`), with
@context@ naming the caller.
declarations.name: gmail_call

anyOf.description:
api_error: An authenticated API call failed for something other than the credential: a non-2xx @status@ that is
not 401 / 403. Which failures are worth repeating is read off @status@ — 408 / 429 / 5xx are the
transient ones, and every other status repeats its answer until the argument changes — which is why
the status rides on the error rather than being folded into a sentence. @context@ says which call
failed in the caller's own words; @message@ carries the server's own body verbatim.

$katari_constructor.description: The tag that selects this variant. Write this exact string.

context.description: Which call failed, in the caller's own words — for a human reading the error (e.g. "tavily.search").

message.description: The response body, or the reason the caller has instead.

anyOf.description:
auth_error: An authenticated API call was rejected over the identity of the caller: the endpoint answered 401 or
403, so the credential is what failed — revoked, expired, or scoped too narrowly. Retrying with the
same credential gives the same answer; the recovery is a fresh resolution of it, so the ordinary
composition is a `supervise` converter signalling `supervise.interrupted`. @context@ says which call
failed in the caller's own words and @message@ carries the server's own body, kept apart so a renderer
can show either alone.

403 is read as auth even though some APIs also spend it on quota exhaustion; a quota 403 that is
replayed answers the same way.

declarations.documentation:
Tool: read a message's body by @id@. Returns a `message_body` — the @text@ and the @content_type@ of the
part it came from, so a reader always knows what it is holding: "text/plain" for an ordinary mail,
"text/html" with the raw markup when the message has no plain-text part (a newsletter, a receipt and
most mail a company sends; expect tags, and expect a long mail to be a long result), or `null` with
Gmail's short snippet preview when it has neither. Attachments are not part of the body — they are listed
on the `message` (`list_recent`) and fetched by `fetch_attachment`.
declarations.name: read_body

for an ordinary mail, "text/html" when the message had no plain-text part (@text@ is then markup, tags
and all), or `null` when it had neither and @text@ is Gmail's short snippet preview.

declarations.checkedType: agent(attachment_id: string, content_type?: string, id: string) -> file with credential | throw[malformed_base64 | api_error | auth_error | fetch_error | parse_error] | io
declarations.documentation:
Tool: fetch one of a message's attachments and return it as a file. @id@ is the message's id (a
`list_recent` result's @id@, not its @message_id@) and @attachment_id@ is the @attachment_id@ of one entry
in that message's @attachments@ list. Pass @content_type@ too — the very `content_type` that listing
showed beside the attachment id: Gmail regenerates attachment ids on every message read, so the fallback
re-read may match no part and hand back an untyped file a receiver sees as a generic `.bin`. The result is
a `file` handle whose bytes stay runtime-side, so it can be passed straight to any other tool you hold
that takes a file while the payload never enters the conversation. The file carries a type but no name, so
a receiver sees a generated one like `file-1.pdf` — say the real filename in your message when it matters.
This only reads, and one call fetches one attachment, so ask for the one you actually need. A payload that
comes back corrupt throws `files.malformed_base64`; a non-2xx reply raises `http.api_failure`
(`http.auth_error` | `http.api_error`).
declarations.name: fetch_attachment

declarations.checkedType: agent(body: string, in_reply_to?: string, subject: string, thread_id?: string, to: string) -> string with credential | throw[api_error | auth_error | fetch_error | parse_error] | io
declarations.documentation:
Tool: send a plain-text email from the authenticated user. @to@ is the recipient address, @subject@ the
subject line, @body@ the message body; it returns the sent message's id, and a sent mail cannot be taken
back. To reply inside a conversation, pass @thread_id@ (a message's `thread_id`, so Gmail files the reply
in that thread) and @in_reply_to@ (that message's `message_id` — its RFC822 `Message-ID` header, not its
`id`), which become the `In-Reply-To` and `References` headers so a mail client threads it too; both
default to `null`, a fresh send. Compose the @subject@ yourself — prefix "Re: " for a reply. The RFC822
message is base64url-encoded into the ordinary `messages.send` `raw` field; a non-2xx reply raises
`http.api_failure` (`http.auth_error` | `http.api_error`).

declarations.checkedType: agent(cursor_at: fresh | resume, deliver_to: agent(value: message) -> null with E2, poll_interval_milliseconds: number, query: string) -> never with credential | throw[api_error | auth_error | fetch_error | parse_error] | get | set | E2 | io
declarations.documentation:
Watch the mailbox for mail that arrives matching a Gmail search @query@ and deliver each new message
once, oldest first, to @deliver_to@ — `poll.subscribe` under a Gmail adapter, so it composes under
`parallel [ … ]` and never resolves (`-> never`). Every @poll_interval_milliseconds@ it searches
`<@query@> after:<cursor>`, hands each unseen message to @deliver_to@, and moves the cursor to that
message's own arrival instant (Gmail's `internalDate`, never the poller's clock). @deliver_to@'s effects
@E@ flow to the caller's handlers unchanged, so a delivery may itself reply or label.

Delivery is at-least-once: the commit lands only after a delivery returns, so a crash or a throw in
between re-delivers exactly that message on the next tick. Build exactly-once at the destination by making
the delivery idempotent on the `message`'s @id@.

@cursor_at@ decides what a restart does and has no default. `poll.resume(key = ...)` keeps the cursor in
the store, so the mail that arrived while the watch was down is delivered, oldest first, on the tick after
it comes back; `poll.fresh()` re-primes on every activation and skips the downtime for good. Two watches
sharing one key overwrite each other's cursor.

What it reports is arrival, not matching: the mail already in the mailbox when the subscription starts is
never delivered, and mail that comes to match @query@ later — an old message you star or mark unread — is
not either, because the search never looks below the cursor. `list_recent` answers that question instead.

No retry is built in — a poll failure propagates and kills the subscription — so compose resilience by
wrapping the watch in a supervise provider. The first poll is one @poll_interval_milliseconds@ in, so a
message arriving just after the watch starts is pending rather than lost.
